The episode is the time-horizon determinant taught by history: monopoly power reflects the elasticity of demand, and the elasticity of demand grows with time, so cartel power erodes on the same clock that substitutes take to build.

Drug policy third, as a cautionary tale in inelastic demand. Interdiction aims to raise street prices of addictive drugs, but established users' demand is inelastic, estimates for heroin and cocaine commonly 0.2 to 0.6, so price increases reduce use modestly while increasing total spending on drugs, and that increased spending finances trafficking violence and is extracted from users partly through property crime. The same arithmetic points policy toward the more elastic margins, initiation by new users, and toward demand-side treatment; it is not the whole of drug policy, but no serious analysis proceeds without it.

Minimum wages fourth, where the elasticity in question is employers' demand for labor. The employment effect of a wage floor is governed by that elasticity: if labor demand is highly elastic, a mandated wage increase prices many workers out; if inelastic, wages rise with small employment loss. For decades economists assumed substantial elasticity; the empirical revolution begun by David Card and Alan Krueger's 1990s studies of New Jersey and Pennsylvania fast-food employment found effects near zero for moderate increases, implying short-run labor-demand elasticities smaller than supposed, and subsequent work continues to contest magnitudes, ranges, and long-run adjustment. The dispute itself illustrates this guide's method: the policy argument is, at bottom, an argument about the size of an elasticity, which is an empirical question, settled by measurement rather than slogan.

sections.heading: Measuring Elasticity: Data, Identification, and Experiments
sections.body:
Estimating an elasticity sounds like curve-fitting: collect prices and quantities, regress the logarithm of quantity on the logarithm of price, read the coefficient. The procedure is genuinely standard, and the log-log regression's slope is indeed an elasticity estimate. The trouble is that the data points were not generated by sliding along one demand curve, and untangling what actually moved is the identification problem, the central methodological challenge of empirical economics.

Observed prices and quantities are equilibrium outcomes, produced by demand and supply jointly. When the price of coffee rises one year and quantity barely falls, the analyst cannot tell whether demand is inelastic or whether demand shifted outward, more coffee drinkers, at the same time supply shifted inward, a frost in Brazil. A naive regression of quantity on price mixes movements of the demand curve with movements along it, and the resulting number is biased toward zero or even positive, an average of demand and supply responses rather than either. The classic demonstration is agricultural: plotting annual corn prices against quantities traces neither curve, but a cloud shaped by weather and income shocks together.

The solution is to isolate variation in price that came from supply alone, an instrumental variable: something that shifts sellers' costs or supply while having no direct effect on buyers' willingness to purchase. Weather is the venerable instrument for crops, a frost moves supply, not tastes. Crude-oil price movements instrument retail gasoline supply; excise-tax changes across states and dates instrument cigarette prices; exchange-rate swings instrument import prices; and in the modern industrial-organization toolkit, cost shifters and the prices of the same product in other markets serve. The logic, formalized in the 1920s and 1930s by Philip Wright and the Cowles Commission economists working on exactly the farm-demand problem, remains the backbone: an elasticity estimate is only as credible as the argument that its price variation was supply-driven.

Where nature provides no instrument, analysts manufacture variation. Firms run pricing experiments outright, raising price in randomly chosen cities or web sessions and reading the elasticity off the treatment-control quantity gap; scanner-data revolutionized this from the 1980s, and e-commerce made it continuous, with A-B price tests now ordinary if reputationally delicate. Governments' natural experiments, tax changes, regulated price resets, tariff shocks, serve the same role in public economics, and the RAND Health Insurance Experiment, which randomized families into insurance plans with different coinsurance from 1974 to 1982, remains the most famous designed measurement of a demand elasticity, health care's 0.2.

Even with clean identification, craft remains. Elasticities differ by segment, horizon, and price level, so a single number is a summary of a surface; dynamic goods, durables, storables, addictives, require models separating purchase timing from consumption; aggregation can mislead, since a category's elasticity is not the average of its brands'; and functional form matters when extrapolating beyond observed prices. Practitioners therefore report ranges, test robustness, and respect an uncomfortable truth: many published elasticities disagree because they measure genuinely different objects. The atlas of numbers earlier in this guide is best read with that humility attached.

sections.heading: Edge Cases and Exceptions: Giffen Goods, Veblen Goods, and Zero Prices
sections.body:
The elasticity framework rests on the law of demand, price up, quantity down, and the law holds with such generality that its exceptions are celebrated like rare birds. They are worth knowing both for their own sake and for what they teach about the machinery underneath.

The Giffen good is the canonical exception: a good whose quantity demanded rises when its price rises, driven not by love of high prices but by the collision of income and substitution effects. The candidate must be an inferior good, one consumed less as income rises, that dominates the budgets of poor consumers and has cheaper calories nowhere else. When the price of the staple rises, the household is made effectively poorer; too poor, now, to afford the meat or vegetables that supplemented the staple, it abandons them and buys more of the staple itself, the only affordable filler. Alfred Marshall attributed the observation to Sir Robert Giffen with bread in Victorian Britain, though evidence for that case is thin; the first rigorous field demonstration came in 2008, when Robert Jensen and Nolan Miller subsidized rice and wheat for poor households in China's Hunan and Gansu provinces and found staple consumption falling as its effective price fell, Giffen behavior in reverse, precisely among households poor enough for the mechanism. The lesson is not that demand curves routinely slope upward, they almost never do, but that the income effect is real and can, in extremis, overpower substitution.

The Veblen good is the apparent exception from the opposite end of the income scale: goods purchased partly because they are expensive, named for Thorstein Veblen's 1899 analysis of conspicuous consumption. When a handbag's price is its message, a price cut can reduce its cachet and its sales. Analytically this is less a violation of the law of demand than a shift of the demand curve caused by the price itself, price entering preferences as a signal of exclusivity and quality, and related phenomena appear wherever price is read as information: consumers inferring that the cheaper wine, lawyer, or medicine must be worse, placebo studies finding branded and pricier painkillers relieving more pain. Sellers of luxury and reputation goods manage these dynamics deliberately, maintaining price floors, destroying unsold stock, and restricting distribution, choices unintelligible under textbook elasticity and routine once price is also a signal.

Zero prices form a third edge, prominent in the digital economy. Elasticity arithmetic breaks at a price of zero, percentage changes from zero are undefined, and behavior breaks too: experiments by Kristina Shampanier, Nina Mazar, and Dan Ariely showed a discontinuous jump in demand when a price falls from one cent to free, the zero-price effect, as if free goods occupy a separate mental category. Free-to-consumer platforms, search, social media, broadcast, therefore monetize the other side of the market, attention sold to advertisers, and the operative elasticities move there. Storage and expectations supply a final set of wrinkles: when buyers expect further price increases, a price rise can temporarily raise purchases of storable goods, hoarding, and panic-buying, an intertemporal substitution masquerading as an upward-sloping demand curve until the pantry fills.

sections.heading: When Elasticity Thinking Goes Wrong: Failure Modes and Good Practice
sections.body:
The concept fails its users in recurring, recognizable ways, and a catalogue of the failure modes is the best inoculation.

Mistaking shifts for movements heads the list. Elasticity describes movement along a demand curve with everything else frozen; in the wild, everything else moves. A retailer who raises prices in November and sees sales climb has not discovered upward-sloping demand, holiday season shifted the curve. The professional defense is explicit controls, comparison groups, or experiments, and the amateur defense is the habit of asking what else changed before crediting any price-quantity pair to elasticity.

Using someone else's elasticity is second. Numbers estimated for another product tier, country, decade, customer segment, or price level transfer poorly: category elasticities understate brand elasticities several-fold, short-run numbers understate long-run ones, and an estimate from the neighborhood of ten dollars says little about behavior at thirty. The most expensive version is extrapolation along one's own curve, raising price repeatedly on the strength of an elasticity measured at lower prices, and discovering, as subscription services and toll roads periodically do, that elasticity grows with each increase until the next one destroys revenue; the New Coke era's scanner studies and the streaming-price escalations of the 2020s both trace this arc.

Confusing revenue with welfare or profit is third. Inelastic demand invites price and tax increases because revenue rises; nothing in that arithmetic says the increase is efficient, fair, or sustainable, and inelastic buyers are often captive buyers, patients, addicts, commuters, tenants, whose inability to escape is precisely why pricing them harder invites regulation, reputational damage, and eventual entry by substitutes; insulin pricing in the United States ran this full circuit to a legislated copay cap in 2022. Symmetrically, elastic demand does not doom price increases when costs or strategy demand them; it prices their consequences.

Static thinking is fourth. Elasticities are endogenous over time: every period of high prices finances the search for substitutes that raises future elasticity, the OPEC lesson, and every improvement in switching technology, comparison sites, generic substitution, number portability, flattens curves industry-wide. Firms and governments that treat today's elasticity as a permanent endowment plan their own surprises. A cousin of this error ignores competitive reaction, applying an own-price elasticity estimated while rivals held prices fixed to a move rivals will certainly match.

The craft that avoids these failures is unglamorous. State the market, segment, horizon, and price neighborhood attached to any number used. Prefer numbers from variation you can defend as supply-driven or experimentally assigned. Re-estimate after any large change, and treat elasticity as a surface to be mapped, not a constant to be quoted. Distinguish the firm's question, residual demand including rivals' response, from the policy question, market demand including entry. And keep the concept in its place: elasticity is a superb summary of how behavior responded to price in a particular time and place, an input to judgment about revenue, incidence, and power, and a substitute for none of the judgment itself. Used with those disciplines, the little ratio Marshall formalized in 1890 remains what it has been for over a century: the sharpest single question to ask about any market.

guides.title: How Prices Carry Information
guides.summary: How a single number compresses the dispersed knowledge of millions of strangers into a signal that coordinates production and consumption — the mechanism, its history, what it does well, and the specific things it cannot do.

sections.heading: The Coordination Problem
sections.body:
Consider an ordinary wooden pencil. The cedar was grown in Oregon or Brazil and felled with saws made of steel from ore mined elsewhere; the graphite came from Sri Lanka or China and was mixed with clay from Mississippi; the ferrule is brass, an alloy of copper and zinc from separate mines; the eraser is a rubber-like compound made partly from rapeseed oil and sulphur chloride. Hundreds of thousands of people contributed to it. Not one of them knows how to make a pencil, and almost none of them knew they were helping. The essayist Leonard Read made this observation the centre of a short 1958 piece titled I, Pencil, and the point survives the passage of time: an object no single mind can design gets made anyway, reliably, cheaply, without anyone in charge.

What coordinates them is a system of prices. The loggers do not need to know that pencils exist. They need to know what cedar fetches this week and what it costs them to cut it. Everything else — the state of demand for pencils in Lagos, a fire in a Chinese graphite plant, a new pencil factory in Vietnam, the opening of a rival cedar plantation — reaches them, if it reaches them at all, as a change in that one number.

This is the central fact about prices, and it is easy to miss because prices feel so ordinary. A price is not principally a measure of value, nor a statement of what something cost to make, nor a moral verdict on what something is worth. A price is a piece of information about relative scarcity, condensed from an enormous quantity of dispersed knowledge into a single scalar that strangers can act on without understanding it. The compression is extreme and it is the point: a functioning market performs, continuously and without instruction, a computation that no committee could perform even in principle, because most of the inputs to that computation exist only as unarticulated local knowledge in millions of separate heads.

This guide traces that mechanism carefully. It begins with the knowledge problem that makes coordination hard, works through what a price actually represents and how markets grope toward one, and follows the argument through the historical debate over whether planners could do without prices. It then examines prices about the future, prices in financial markets, and the categories of thing prices systematically fail to capture — external costs, hidden quality, public goods, and the distribution of purchasing power itself. It closes with what happens when the signal is suppressed and how to read prices without over-reading them.

The honest position throughout is neither that markets are magic nor that they are arbitrary. The informational argument for prices is one of the strongest results in social science, and the catalogue of its limits is equally well established. Both halves are necessary; holding only one is how people end up confidently wrong about policy.

sections.heading: Hayek and the Knowledge Problem
sections.body:
The clearest statement of the argument appeared in September 1945, when Friedrich Hayek published The Use of Knowledge in Society in the American Economic Review. Hayek was arguing against a view then widely held: that the economic problem was essentially one of computation, and that a sufficiently well-informed central authority could solve it better than a chaotic market.

His objection was not about computing power. It was about where the relevant knowledge lives. Hayek distinguished scientific or technical knowledge, which can be written down and centralised, from what he called the knowledge of the particular circumstances of time and place — that a machine in a particular shop is running below capacity this week, that a supplier is quietly unreliable, that a certain warehouse has stock nobody has catalogued, that a customer will accept a substitute. This knowledge is enormous in aggregate, held only in fragments, often not consciously articulated even by the person who holds it, and frequently obsolete within days. It cannot be gathered into one place because much of it does not exist in transmissible form.

His illustration is worth following exactly, because it is the whole argument in miniature. Suppose tin becomes scarcer — either a new use has been found for it, or a source has been lost. It does not matter which, and Hayek's key claim is that almost nobody needs to know which. Users of tin learn only that they must economise; some substitute aluminium, some redesign a product, some draw down inventory. Their reduced buying and increased buying of substitutes moves other prices, and the disturbance propagates outward through the whole economy, dying away as it goes. The people at the far edge of the ripple adjust correctly to a shortage they never heard about, in a metal they may not use, caused by an event they could not name.

Hayek's phrase for the price system was a mechanism for communicating information, and he called it marvellous chiefly because of how little each participant needs to know. The person acting needs one number and their own local circumstances. The system economises on knowledge, which is the scarcest input of all.

Two cautions belong with the argument. First, Hayek was describing a tendency, not a guarantee; nothing in it says the adjustment is instant, complete, or fair. Second, the argument is informational rather than moral. It explains why decentralised coordination outperforms central direction at certain tasks. It does not establish that whatever a market produces is good, and Hayek's own writings on when markets fail are less quoted than they deserve to be.

It is also worth noticing what the argument implies about scale, because this is where it bites hardest. A workshop of twenty people can be planned. The difficulty grows not linearly but explosively with the number of distinct goods, because what must be coordinated is the relationships between them. A modern economy handles hundreds of millions of distinguishable products, and the knowledge required to allocate them is regenerated continuously. The price system solves this not by being clever but by not needing the knowledge in one place at all.

sections.heading: What a Price Actually Represents
sections.body:
To see what information a price carries, it helps to be precise about what the number means, because the everyday intuition — that price reflects how much work went into something — is not merely incomplete but actively misleading.

A market price is the rate at which the marginal buyer and the marginal seller are just willing to trade. Both words matter. Marginal means the last unit, not the average or the first: the price of bread is set by what the person most nearly indifferent about buying one more loaf will pay, not by how desperately a starving person values their first. Just willing means the price sits at the point where the most eager remaining seller and the most eager remaining buyer meet; everyone above and below that point has already traded or has stayed out.

This resolves a puzzle that defeated economists for a century. Adam Smith, writing in 1776, noted that water is essential to life and nearly free while diamonds are useless and enormously expensive, and could not fully explain it. The answer arrived independently in the early 1870s, from Carl Menger in Vienna in 1871, William Stanley Jevons in Manchester in the same year, and Léon Walras in Lausanne in 1874 — the marginal revolution. Value in exchange depends not on total usefulness but on the usefulness of one more unit at the current level of abundance. Water is abundant, so the marginal litre does little for you; diamonds are scarce, so the marginal stone is a prize. Change the abundance and the price follows: water in a desert is priced like a diamond.

The consequence is that price is forward-looking and cost is backward-looking. What was spent producing something is sunk and cannot influence what anyone will pay for it. A ship built for a route that no longer exists is worth its scrap value regardless of what it cost. Costs matter, but through a different channel: they determine what suppliers are willing to keep producing, and therefore how much reaches the market, and therefore where the marginal seller sits.

The information content follows directly. If the price of copper rises, it is telling everyone that somewhere in the world, copper has become harder to get relative to how much people want it — nothing more specific, and nothing less real. The signal is anonymous, quantitative and comparable across completely unrelated activities, which is precisely what allows a farmer, a shipbuilder and a chip designer to make coherent decisions about the same metal without ever meeting.

One further precision matters. Because every price is quoted in money, a change in a single price can mean two different things. It can be relative — this good has become scarcer compared with others, which is information. Or it can be part of a general change in the value of money, in which case all prices are moving together and the information content is near zero. Confusing the two is the commonest error in reading prices, and it is why economists distinguish nominal figures from real ones.

sections.heading: How a Market Finds a Price
sections.body:
Prices are not announced. They are discovered, through a process of trial, disappointment and adjustment that is worth watching closely because the discovery itself is where the information gets in.

Start with a mismatch. Suppose a seller sets a price and finds their stock gone by noon every day with queues forming. That is a shortage, and it carries a message: the price is below the level at which the quantity people want equals the quantity available. The seller raises it. Some buyers drop out — specifically, the ones who valued the good least, since anyone valuing it above the new price still buys — and the queue shortens. Conversely, unsold inventory piling up is a surplus, and the seller cuts the price until the least eager sellers withdraw and buyers return. The price stops moving when neither queues nor gluts appear, which is what economists mean by market clearing.

Léon Walras described this as tâtonnement, French for groping, and imagined an auctioneer calling out prices until no excess demand remained. Real markets have no auctioneer, and the groping is done by thousands of participants adjusting independently, which is slower and messier but has the same logic. Financial exchanges come closest to the idealisation: a limit order book displays every bid and offer, and trades execute where they cross, continuously, in microseconds.

The crucial feature is that this process aggregates information nobody stated. A buyer who quietly drops out at a higher price has revealed something about their circumstances without saying a word or being asked. A supplier who ramps up production because the margin has widened has acted on a signal without knowing its cause. Every transaction and every refusal to transact adds a data point, and the price is the running summary.

Formal economics eventually proved that such an equilibrium exists under stated conditions. Kenneth Arrow and Gérard Debreu published an existence proof in 1954, and the associated welfare theorems establish that a competitive equilibrium is efficient in a limited sense — no one can be made better off without making someone worse off. Be honest about how much those results assume: complete markets for every good in every state of the world, no externalities, no market power, perfectly informed participants. None hold exactly anywhere. The theorems are best read as a precise statement of the conditions under which the informational argument works, and therefore as a map of where it breaks. They also say nothing about whether real markets converge, or how fast; stability is a separate and much less settled question.

Discovery costs something, which is why market design matters. An auction, a posted-price shop and a continuous exchange are different institutions for finding the same number, differing in speed and in who bears the cost of searching. Where discovery is expensive — houses, used machinery, freelance labour — prices are noisy and dispersed, and two nearly identical items can trade at very different prices in the same week. The tightness of a price is itself information about how well its market works.

sections.heading: The Dual Role: Signal and Incentive
sections.body:
A price does three jobs at once, and much confused argument about markets comes from noticing one and forgetting the others. It informs, it motivates, and it rations. These are inseparable in a market price and separable in principle, which is exactly what makes policy hard.

As a signal, a price tells you the relative scarcity of a thing. As an incentive, it makes acting on that signal worth your while: a high price for copper does not merely inform a miner that copper is scarce, it pays them to go and get more of it, and pays a manufacturer to use less. As a rationing device, it settles who gets the limited quantity that actually exists — namely, those willing to pay the price.

The strength of the arrangement is that all three point the same way. The signal is credible precisely because acting on it is costly: a seller who claims scarcity but will not hold out for a higher price is not believed, and a buyer who claims to want something badly but will not pay is not accommodated. Talk is cheap; prices are statements backed by money, which is why they aggregate honest information where surveys of intentions do not.

The weakness is that the rationing job carries a distributional consequence that the informational argument does not address. A price rations by willingness to pay, and willingness to pay reflects both how much someone wants something and how much money they have. Two people can want water equally and only one can bid for it. This is not a flaw in the mechanism's logic; it is a fact about what the mechanism measures. The price system aggregates preferences weighted by purchasing power, and any conclusion drawn from prices inherits that weighting.

This is the honest core of most disputes about markets. When someone objects to a price rising sharply after a disaster, they are usually objecting to the rationing function, while the person defending it is usually pointing at the signalling and incentive functions. Both are describing the same number. A high post-hurricane price for generators does genuinely pull generators toward the disaster area from hundreds of miles away and does genuinely stop the first arrivals from buying four each — and it does genuinely mean that the poorest households get none. Recognising that these are three effects of one number, rather than one effect that is simply good or simply bad, is most of what it takes to think clearly about the subject.

The separability point matters for policy design. Because the three functions are conceptually distinct, it is sometimes possible to keep the signal and the incentive while changing the rationing. Letting the price rise and transferring cash to those who cannot afford it preserves the information and fixes the distribution; capping the price destroys the information and creates a shortage that must then be rationed by queueing, connections or luck instead. Which of those is preferable in a given case is a real argument, but it is a much better argument than one conducted as though the price were only ever one thing.

sections.heading: Profit, Loss and the Feedback Loop
sections.body:
Prices coordinate at a moment. What makes an economy improve over time is the feedback that profits and losses provide, and this is a distinct mechanism worth separating from the signalling one.

A firm buys inputs at their prices and sells output at its price. The difference, profit, is a compact verdict on whether the firm's activity was worth doing: it says that the bundle of resources consumed was valued by others less than the thing produced from them. A loss says the reverse — that the resources were worth more in some other use, and the firm has destroyed value by combining them this way. Because both sides of the comparison are expressed in the same units, the verdict is quantitative and comparable across completely unlike activities.

This is why profit and loss are best understood as an error-correction system rather than as a reward scheme. Losses force the release of misallocated resources; that is their function, and it is why shielding firms from losses indefinitely tends to freeze resources in low-value uses. Profits do the opposite, drawing resources toward activities others value more, and in competitive conditions they are self-limiting: high profits attract entrants, entry expands supply, supply lowers price, and the profit erodes. Persistently high profits are therefore usually evidence of a barrier — a patent, a licence, a network effect, a genuine scarcity, or a lack of competitors — rather than of ordinary success.

The entrepreneurial reading of this, associated with Israel Kirzner, is that the signal a market really sends is not just the current price but the gap between prices — the observation that something is cheap here and dear there, or that inputs available at one price could be recombined into something people would pay more for. Acting on such a gap both earns profit and closes it, so the pursuit of profit is simultaneously the mechanism by which the system discovers and eliminates its own errors.

The feedback loop has real limitations and they are not marginal. It works only where the person collecting the profit bears the corresponding costs, which is precisely what externalities violate. It operates on the time horizon of the decision-maker, which can be far shorter than the horizon of the consequences. It rewards the discovery of ways to capture value as readily as ways to create it — lobbying for a favourable rule and inventing a better product both show up as profit, and the accounts do not distinguish them. Any serious account of markets has to hold the correction mechanism and these failure channels in view together.

There is also a quieter informational role for accounting prices inside organisations. A large firm is itself a planned economy, and when its divisions trade with one another it must invent transfer prices to compare uses of shared resources. Those internal prices are not discovered by trading and are frequently gamed, which is why divisional accounting is a perennial source of dysfunction in big companies — a small-scale rehearsal of exactly the calculation problem that planners face at national scale.

sections.heading: The Socialist Calculation Debate
sections.body:
The informational theory of prices was not developed in the abstract. It emerged from a decades-long argument about whether a planned economy could function without markets, and that argument remains the sharpest test of the theory because it produced real experiments.

Ludwig von Mises opened it in 1920 with an essay on economic calculation in the socialist commonwealth. His claim was not that planners would be lazy or wicked but that they would be blind. Without markets in capital goods, there are no prices for capital goods; without such prices, there is no common unit in which to compare, say, building a railway out of steel against building bridges out of the same steel. Planners could count tonnes, but tonnes of different things are not commensurable, and the choice among technically feasible plans becomes arbitrary.

The most sophisticated reply came from Oskar Lange in 1936 and 1937, developed further by Abba Lerner. Lange accepted that prices were necessary but denied that markets were the only way to get them. A central board could publish trial prices, instruct managers to produce where marginal cost equalled that price, watch inventories, and adjust — Walras's tâtonnement performed administratively. On paper this works, and for a generation many economists considered the matter settled in Lange's favour.

Hayek's response, of which the 1945 paper is the distillation, was that the reply conceded the wrong point. The problem was never solving a system of equations given the data; it was that the data do not exist in collectable form, are generated by the act of competing, and change continuously. A board adjusting prices from inventory reports is always reacting to a world that has moved.

The historical record is suggestive rather than decisive, and should be read carefully. Soviet planning set millions of prices administratively and coexisted with chronic shortages of ordinary goods, elaborate informal exchange, and severe misallocation, though it also achieved rapid industrialisation. Chile's Project Cybersyn, built by Stafford Beer between 1971 and 1973, attempted real-time telex-based coordination and was ended by the coup before it could be evaluated. Meanwhile the planning tradition produced genuinely valuable tools: Leonid Kantorovich's linear programming, developed from 1939, generates shadow prices that carry exactly the scarcity information Mises demanded, and earned him a share of the 1975 Nobel Prize. The debate's most durable result is not that planning is impossible but that any large-scale allocation system needs scarcity prices from somewhere, and that generating them without decentralised trading has proved extremely hard.

The debate has revived in recent years on new grounds. Some argue that modern computation, continuous data from retail and logistics systems, and machine learning have finally supplied what Lange lacked, and point to the internal planning systems of very large firms as evidence that enormous supply chains can be directed administratively. Critics reply that those firms still buy and sell at market prices at their boundaries, and so remain parasitic on the surrounding price system for their scarcity information. The question is genuinely open, and anyone who tells you it was settled decades ago is overstating what the evidence supports in either direction.

sections.heading: Prices About the Future
sections.body:
A spot price reports present scarcity. A futures price does something stranger and more useful: it reports the market's aggregated expectation about scarcity at a stated date months or years ahead, and it does so in a way that forces the people making the forecast to stake money on it.

A futures contract is an agreement to buy or sell a standardised quantity of something at a fixed price on a fixed future date. Because such contracts trade continuously, their prices form a curve running out into the future — the price of oil for delivery next month, in six months, in two years. The shape of that curve is itself information. When distant contracts trade above near ones, a condition called contango, the market is signalling either abundant present supply or the expectation of future tightness, and it is paying storage operators to hold inventory rather than sell it. When distant contracts trade below near ones, called backwardation, present scarcity is acute and holders are being paid to release stock now. Traders read that shape the way a doctor reads a chart.

The forecasting quality is genuinely good on average and genuinely unreliable in any single instance. Futures markets aggregate the views of people who lose money by being wrong, which filters out cheap talk in a way that opinion polling and expert panels cannot. But a futures price is not a prediction of the spot price; it also embeds storage costs, interest rates, and a risk premium paid by those who want to hedge rather than speculate. Extracting a pure forecast from it requires stripping those out, and the residual error is large.

The same logic underlies prediction markets, in which contracts pay a fixed sum if a stated event occurs, so that the price sits between zero and one and reads directly as a probability. The Iowa Electronic Markets, running since 1988 on US elections, have often outperformed contemporaneous polls, and corporate internal markets have been used to forecast product launch dates more accurately than management estimates, plausibly because a trader loses money for flattery while a subordinate does not. Their known weaknesses are thin volume in obscure questions, a documented bias toward overpricing low-probability events, and vulnerability to manipulation when the stakes outside the market exceed the money inside it.

There is a deeper limit. A market can only price what someone will write a contract on, and the most consequential future events are often the ones nobody thought to name. The absence of a price is not the absence of a risk, and reading a quiet futures curve as reassurance is a specific and recurring mistake.

Forward-looking prices also feed directly back into the present, which is what makes them powerful and occasionally destabilising. A high futures price for a crop persuades farmers to plant more of it, and the planting itself then lowers the future price the forecast was based on. Economists call this reflexivity, and in agriculture it produces the classic cobweb cycle of alternating gluts and shortages. A price about the future is never a neutral observation of it.

sections.heading: Financial Prices and the Efficiency Question
sections.body:
Financial markets are the purest case of prices as information, because a share or a bond is nothing but a claim on future money, and its price is therefore almost entirely a summary of beliefs. That makes them the natural laboratory for testing how much information a price actually contains.

The canonical statement is Eugene Fama's efficient market hypothesis, set out in a 1970 review. A market is efficient if prices fully reflect available information, and Fama distinguished three strengths: weak form, in which prices already reflect all past price history so technical patterns cannot be traded profitably; semi-strong, in which they reflect all public information so analysing published accounts cannot; and strong, in which they reflect private information too. The weak and semi-strong forms have substantial empirical support, and the practical consequence is real — the persistent difficulty most professional fund managers have in beating a broad index after fees is exactly what the theory predicts, and it is the reason index funds exist.

The hypothesis contains a paradox that Sanford Grossman and Joseph Stiglitz stated formally in 1980. If prices already reflected all information, nobody would have any incentive to gather information, since gathering is costly and the payoff is zero. But if nobody gathers, prices reflect nothing. A market therefore cannot be perfectly efficient: it must remain slightly inefficient, by just enough to pay the people whose research makes it efficient. Efficiency is best understood as an equilibrium level of imperfection maintained by competition, not an absolute property.

The evidence for the strong form is poor, and its failure is legible in enforcement statistics: insider trading is profitable, which is precisely why it is illegal. The evidence on longer horizons is genuinely contested. Robert Shiller argued from the early 1980s that share prices move far more than the underlying stream of dividends can justify, implying that something other than information drives much of the variation. The 2013 Nobel Prize was awarded jointly to Fama, Lars Peter Hansen and Shiller, and Fama and Shiller substantially disagree — an unusually candid acknowledgement by a prize committee that the question is not resolved. Behavioural research since the 1980s has catalogued systematic patterns in how people misjudge probability, and the open question is how far competition among sophisticated traders cancels those errors out rather than amplifying them.

Episodes of dramatic mispricing are part of the record and should not be explained away: the South Sea affair of 1720, the technology share boom that broke in 2000, and the housing and mortgage-security valuations that collapsed from 2007. Even the Dutch tulip mania of 1637, the standard morality tale, is now thought by historians such as Anne Goldgar to have been far smaller and less economically damaging than legend records — a reminder that stories about market madness are themselves subject to inflation.

sections.heading: What Prices Leave Out: External Costs
sections.body:
The informational argument depends on a hidden assumption: that the price of a thing reflects all the costs of producing it. Where it does not, the signal is not merely incomplete but systematically wrong, and everyone acting on it is being efficiently coordinated toward the wrong outcome.

An externality is a cost or benefit that falls on someone outside the transaction. A factory that emits particulates imposes illness on people downwind who neither bought nor sold anything; a driver in traffic imposes delay on every other driver; a vaccinated person confers protection on neighbours who did not pay for it. In each case the price the participants face omits part of the real consequence, so the market produces too much of the thing with unpriced costs and too little of the thing with unpriced benefits. This is not a failure of the mechanism to work; it is the mechanism working correctly on incorrect input.

Arthur Pigou set out the standard analysis in The Economics of Welfare in 1920 and proposed the standard remedy: a tax equal to the external cost, which puts the missing information back into the price and restores the signal without dictating how anyone should respond. A carbon price is the leading modern application, whether levied as a tax or created by capping emissions and letting permits trade, as the European Union's emissions trading system has done since 2005. The design intent is precisely informational — nobody is told how to cut emissions; they are told what emitting costs, and left to find the cheapest reductions themselves.

Ronald Coase reframed the problem in 1960. His argument was that if property rights are clear and bargaining is costless, the affected parties will negotiate to an efficient outcome regardless of who holds the right — the polluter may pay to pollute or the neighbours may pay for quiet, but the quantity will be the same. The often-missed point is that Coase regarded costless bargaining as unrealistic; his real conclusion was that transaction costs determine which institutional arrangement works best, and that the choice between markets, regulation and courts is empirical rather than ideological.

The practical obstacles are large and honest description requires stating them. Measuring an external cost is genuinely hard, and estimates of the social cost of a tonne of carbon dioxide have spanned an order of magnitude across credible studies, largely because the result depends on ethical choices about how to weigh future generations. Setting the price too low leaves most of the distortion in place, and setting it high enough to matter is politically difficult everywhere it has been tried.

Not every externality problem needs a price. Elinor Ostrom, who received the 2009 Nobel Prize, documented hundreds of communities — irrigation systems, fisheries, alpine pastures — that governed shared resources sustainably for centuries through negotiated rules, monitoring and graduated sanctions, without either private ownership or a central authority. Her work is a corrective to the assumption that the only alternatives are markets and states.

sections.heading: Hidden Quality and Asymmetric Information
sections.body:
A price can also carry the wrong information when one side of a trade knows something the other does not. The consequences are more severe than intuition suggests: markets do not merely become less efficient, they can collapse entirely, and the ones that vanish are frequently the ones society most needs.

George Akerlof's 1970 paper on the market for lemons demonstrated the mechanism with used cars. Suppose sellers know whether a car is sound and buyers do not. Buyers can only offer a price reflecting average quality. Owners of genuinely good cars find that price insulting and withdraw, which lowers the average quality of what remains, which lowers the price buyers will offer, which drives out the next tier of sellers. The process can iterate until only the worst goods trade, or until no trade occurs at all. The market unravels not because anyone behaved badly but because the price cannot distinguish what it needs to distinguish.

Two families of remedy exist, and both are ways of restoring the missing information. Signalling, analysed by Michael Spence, has the informed party take a costly action that would not be worth taking if their claim were false — an unconditional warranty is cheap for someone selling a sound car and ruinous for someone selling a wreck, so offering one is credible in a way that saying the car is fine is not. Spence's original application was education as a signal of ability, independent of anything learned. Screening, analysed by Joseph Stiglitz, has the uninformed party design choices that sort people: an insurer offering a menu of deductibles learns something real about a customer's risk from which one they pick. Akerlof, Spence and Stiglitz shared the 2001 Nobel Prize for this body of work.

The pattern recurs wherever quality is hard to observe. Health insurance suffers adverse selection because the sick know more about their health than the insurer, which is one of the standard arguments for mandatory or universal coverage. Credit markets ration by refusing loans rather than raising rates, because a higher rate selects for riskier borrowers. Labour markets rely heavily on credentials for the same reason.

The general lesson for reading prices is that a price only summarises quality when quality is observable or credibly certified. Where it is not, a low price may indicate a bargain or a defect, and the market cannot tell you which. This is why brands, warranties, licensing, reviews, inspections and reputation systems exist: they are institutions built to supply the information the price alone cannot carry.

One subtlety runs the other way and is worth naming. Because buyers know that price sometimes tracks quality, a high price can itself function as a signal, and this can be exploited. Deliberately pricing a product above its rivals in order to suggest superiority works precisely because quality is unobservable, and in some studies people report greater enjoyment of an identical wine when told it is expensive. Here the price is not transmitting information about scarcity at all; it is manufacturing a belief.

sections.heading: Missing Markets and the Weighting Problem
sections.body:
Two further categories of thing lie beyond what prices can register, and both are structural rather than accidental. One concerns goods that markets cannot supply at all; the other concerns whose preferences the price is counting.

Public goods are those that are non-rival, meaning one person's use does not diminish another's, and non-excludable, meaning you cannot practically stop non-payers from benefiting. National defence, a lighthouse, basic scientific research, a stable legal system and clean air all qualify to varying degrees. Because non-payers cannot be excluded, everyone has an incentive to wait for someone else to fund them, so the market price that emerges is far below the value the good actually delivers, and often no market emerges at all. The absence of a price here reflects an institutional impossibility, not an absence of value, and this is one of the least contested arguments for collective provision in the whole of economics.

Missing markets appear elsewhere for other reasons. Nobody can buy the wellbeing of a person who will exist in a century, so the interests of future people enter markets only through the imperfect proxy of interest rates. Some markets are deliberately forbidden on moral grounds — in votes, in organs, in people — and the argument for those prohibitions is that treating certain things as priced commodities corrupts them, a position economics as such cannot settle either way.

The weighting problem is subtler and more pervasive. A price aggregates willingness to pay, and willingness to pay is jointly determined by preference and by budget. A market therefore counts the wishes of a rich person more heavily than those of a poor person, not through any bias in the mechanism but because that is arithmetically what summing money bids does. When a city's housing market prices out its nurses, the market is not malfunctioning: it is faithfully reporting that other bidders have more money. When pharmaceutical research concentrates on conditions of wealthy populations rather than on diseases that kill more people in poorer ones, the same arithmetic is at work.

None of this argues against using prices. It argues for reading them accurately. A price is a wealth-weighted aggregate of the preferences of those able to participate in that particular market, computed over the costs that were actually charged to the participants. Every one of those qualifications is doing work, and treating the resulting number as a measure of social value simply discards them.

There is a constructive response available that keeps the mechanism while fixing the weighting, and it is worth knowing because it is often overlooked in polarised debate. If the objection is to who can bid rather than to bidding as such, then transferring purchasing power — through cash payments, vouchers, subsidised access or a floor income — changes the weighting while leaving the informational machinery intact. Prices continue to guide production, but a different set of preferences gets counted. Whether that beats direct provision varies by good: it works well for food and poorly for health care, where the asymmetric-information problems are severe enough that a voucher does not fix them.

sections.heading: Suppressing the Signal: Price Controls
sections.body:
The clearest evidence that prices carry information comes from what happens when they are prevented from moving. Price controls are a natural experiment that has been run hundreds of times across thousands of years, and the results are consistent enough to be genuinely informative — though not as simple as either side of the argument usually claims.

A binding price ceiling holds a price below the level that would clear the market. The immediate effect is that quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, and since the price can no longer do the rationing, something else must. Queues appear, as they did at American petrol stations during the price-controlled shortages of 1973 to 1974 and again in 1979, where drivers spent hours in line — a real cost, borne in time instead of money, that benefits nobody. Quality degrades, because with buyers queuing there is no reason to maintain it. Informal markets appear, and allocation shifts toward personal connections. Most importantly, the suppressed price stops telling producers to produce more, so the shortage persists rather than curing itself.

Rent control is the best-studied case, and the honest summary is more nuanced than the standard denunciation. A careful study of San Francisco's 1994 expansion by Rebecca Diamond, Tim McQuade and Franklin Qian, published in 2019, found that it delivered substantial and real benefits to the tenants who were covered, reducing displacement — and that landlords responded by converting or redeveloping properties, reducing the rental housing supply by around fifteen per cent and pushing up rents for everyone not covered. Both findings are the same study. Controls transfer to incumbents and tax entrants, and reasonable people can hold different views about that trade while agreeing on the mechanism.

Price floors invert the pattern: a minimum above the clearing level produces surpluses, which is why agricultural support programmes have historically accumulated stockpiles. Minimum wages are the contested case, and the honest position is that the simple model predicts job losses while a large body of empirical work, beginning with David Card and Alan Krueger in 1994, has often found small or negligible employment effects at moderate levels — which is usually explained by employer wage-setting power. The disagreement is real and unresolved at higher levels.

Anti-gouging laws after disasters occupy contested ground precisely because the three functions of a price conflict most sharply there. Letting the price of generators or bottled water spike does pull supply toward the affected area from far away and does stop early buyers from hoarding; it also means the poorest households are outbid at the worst possible moment. Most jurisdictions have decided that the distributional harm outweighs the supply benefit over the days involved, which is a defensible judgement so long as it is made with the trade-off in view rather than by pretending the supply effect is imaginary.

The general principle survives all the nuance. Controlling a price does not remove the underlying scarcity; it removes the information about it, and the scarcity then expresses itself through queues, shortages, quality decline and informal allocation instead.

sections.heading: Sticky Prices and Non-Market Coordination
sections.body:
Real prices do not behave like the smooth continuous variables of the theory. They sit still for long stretches, jump in discrete steps, and are frequently set by rules of thumb. Understanding this stickiness matters, because it is one of the main reasons economies experience recessions rather than smoothly adjusting.

Surveys of how firms actually set prices — the best known is Alan Blinder's interview study of American companies published in 1998 — find that the median firm changes its prices only about once or twice a year, and that managers give reasons the textbook does not anticipate. Changing prices annoys regular customers and risks appearing exploitative; contracts fix prices for months; competitors' responses are uncertain; and the administrative bother, which economists call menu costs, is not trivial. The practical consequence is that when demand falls, the first response is usually to cut output and lay off workers rather than to cut prices — which is how a fall in spending turns into a fall in employment.

Stickiness is more severe in wages than in most other prices. Employers resist cutting nominal pay even in downturns, partly because it destroys morale and productivity, so labour markets clear through unemployment rather than through falling wages. Whether this justifies active monetary policy is one of the enduring divides in macroeconomics, but the underlying observation is not seriously disputed.

The other great departure from textbook markets is that an enormous share of economic activity is not coordinated by prices at all. Ronald Coase asked in 1937 why, if markets allocate so well, firms exist as islands of conscious planning inside them. His answer was transaction costs: negotiating, contracting and policing a market exchange costs something, and where that cost exceeds the cost of simply instructing someone, the activity moves inside a firm. The boundary of a firm is therefore set by a comparison between two coordination technologies, and large firms are internally planned economies of considerable size.

Modern technology has pushed the boundary in both directions at once. Algorithmic pricing lets retailers and airlines change prices constantly and individually, making some prices far less sticky than they have ever been, while also raising genuine concerns that pricing algorithms may learn to sustain high prices without any explicit agreement between competitors. At the same time, better information systems have made very large internally planned supply chains workable. Neither trend settles the old argument; both change its terms.

A great deal of allocation happens with no price at all, and it is worth remembering how much. Households distribute food, care and labour by custom and affection; queues allocate emergency rooms by triage; lotteries allocate school places; seniority allocates shifts; reciprocity allocates favours. These mechanisms have their own information problems and their own virtues, and the choice among them is one of the most consequential design decisions any institution makes. The price system is one option in that menu rather than the default state of the world.

sections.heading: Reading Prices in Practice
sections.body:
All of this becomes useful only if it changes how you interpret a number you actually encounter. The discipline is to ask what a price is telling you and, just as importantly, what it cannot be telling you. A short diagnostic sequence prevents most of the standard errors.

The habit worth cultivating is scepticism about narrative. Financial journalism supplies a cause for every move, and most of those attributions are unfalsifiable stories fitted after the fact to a number that would have moved anyway. The price is the reliable part; the explanation attached to it usually is not. Conversely, when a price does not move in the face of dramatic news, that too is information — it generally means the news was already expected and had been incorporated before it was announced, which is why markets so often fail to react to headlines that seem enormous.

The same discipline applies to prices you set rather than observe. If you are pricing your own work or your own goods, the number you choose is a message: it rations who approaches you, it signals quality to people who cannot evaluate you directly, and it determines whether you can afford to keep supplying. Setting it from your costs alone ignores two of the three functions, which is why so much undercharging persists even among people who are busy.
steps: Ask first whether the change is relative or general. If nearly everything is rising at once, you are probably observing the value of money changing rather than any change in the scarcity of the particular good, and the informational content about that good is close to zero.

Separate the three functions. Decide whether the change matters to you as information about scarcity, as an incentive to alter your own behaviour, or as a rationing outcome affecting who gets the good — the answer determines which response makes sense.

Check whether the market is one where discovery works. Many participants, frequent trades, standardised goods and public quotes make a price trustworthy; thin, infrequent, bespoke markets produce noisy prices in which a single transaction proves very little.

Ask what costs are excluded. If production imposes pollution, congestion, depletion or risk on people outside the transaction, the price is understating the true cost by an amount nobody has measured, and comparisons against alternatives are correspondingly distorted.

Ask whether quality is observable. Where it is not, a low price may mean a bargain or a defect, and you need an independent source of information — a warranty, an inspection, a reputation — before the price means anything about value.

Distinguish a price about now from a price about the future. Futures, share prices and interest rates are aggregated expectations, so they change when beliefs change, and a move tells you the consensus was revised rather than that anything physical happened yet.

Finally, ask who was able to bid. A price aggregates only the preferences of those with both access to the market and money in it, so a price can be perfectly informative about that population and silent about everyone else.

sections.heading: Failure Modes, Limits and Honest Conclusions
sections.body:
The informational theory of prices is among the more robust findings in social science, and the specific ways it fails are equally well documented. Holding both together is the whole skill.

The characteristic failure of the theory's admirers is over-extension: treating a price as a measure of worth rather than of scarcity-under-current-conditions, concluding that whatever the market produces is therefore right, and forgetting that the efficiency theorems assume conditions no real market satisfies. This error is easy to make because the mechanism genuinely is impressive at what it does, and impressive mechanisms invite over-application. The characteristic failure of the theory's critics is the mirror image: noticing that markets misprice and concluding that prices can simply be overridden by decree, which reliably reproduces the shortages, queues and informal allocation that suppressed signals always produce.

There are also genuine unresolved questions, and it is more useful to name them than to paper over them. How efficient financial markets actually are at long horizons is contested by serious economists on both sides. Whether modern computation changes the calculation debate is an open empirical question rather than a settled one. How much of observed price movement reflects information and how much reflects herding, narrative and liquidity is not known with precision. Whether algorithmic pricing will erode competition is an active area of research with no consensus.

What can be said with confidence is narrower and still substantial. Dispersed local knowledge is real, large and mostly untransmittable, and any allocation system must somehow use it. Prices are the only mechanism yet found that uses it at the scale of a whole economy without requiring anyone to collect it. That mechanism works well where costs are internalised, quality is observable, participants are numerous and the good is excludable and rival. It works badly or not at all where those conditions fail, and the failures are not exotic edge cases — pollution, health care, education, housing, financial risk and climate are among the largest things societies deal with.

It is also worth being clear that the argument is about coordination rather than about morality or politics. Nothing in the informational theory of prices tells you how income should be distributed, what a society owes its members, or which activities are worth pursuing. It is a claim about how a particular kind of computation gets performed, and it is compatible with a very wide range of political arrangements — which is precisely why economies that differ enormously in their tax rates, welfare systems and public sectors all use prices to allocate most ordinary goods. Treating the mechanism as though it entailed a political programme is a category error committed with equal enthusiasm by its supporters and its opponents.

The practical conclusion is unglamorous. Prices are an extraordinary instrument with a precisely known range of validity, like a thermometer that is accurate between stated limits. The competent user reads them carefully within that range, uses other instruments outside it, and never mistakes the reading for the thing itself.

guides.title: Price Elasticity of Supply
guides.summary: How responsive the quantity producers offer is to a change in price, how the measure is calculated and interpreted, and what determines it. Covers time horizons, capacity, storage and entry, the arithmetic of tax incidence, how elasticities are estimated from real data, and where the concept breaks down.

sections.heading: What the Measure Captures and Why It Matters
sections.body:
When the price of something rises, producers generally want to supply more of it. The question that matters for almost every practical problem in economics is: how much more, and how quickly. Price elasticity of supply is the number that answers it. It measures the percentage change in the quantity producers are willing and able to sell, divided by the percentage change in price that provoked it. A value of 2 means a ten percent price rise brings forth a twenty percent increase in quantity supplied. A value of 0.1 means the same price rise brings forth only one percent more, so the market clears almost entirely through price rather than through quantity.

The distinction sounds technical and is not. It decides who pays a tax, how much a subsidy actually increases output, whether a demand boom shows up as more goods or merely as higher prices, how long a shortage lasts, and whether a price control produces a queue. If supply is highly elastic, a surge in demand is absorbed by producers making more, and prices barely move. If supply is inelastic, the same surge is absorbed entirely by price, and the extra money flows to whoever already owns the scarce thing. This is why housing costs behave so differently in Houston and San Francisco given the same influx of workers, and why a poor harvest can double a crop's price while a good one can halve it.

Elasticity is expressed as a ratio of percentages rather than as a slope, and that is a deliberate choice with a specific advantage: it is a pure number, free of units. The slope of a supply curve depends on whether quantity is measured in tonnes or kilograms and price in dollars or cents, so slopes cannot be compared across markets. Elasticities can. An elasticity of 0.4 for crude oil and 0.4 for rental housing mean the same thing about responsiveness even though the underlying units share nothing.

Supply elasticity is conventionally positive, because supply curves normally slope upward: higher prices make production more profitable, cover the costs of marginal producers, and draw in resources from elsewhere. There are genuine exceptions, of which the best documented is the backward-bending labour supply curve, where at high enough wages some workers respond to a further rise by working fewer hours, because the income effect of being richer outweighs the substitution effect of leisure becoming more expensive. Such cases are real but unusual, and unless stated otherwise the elasticity of supply should be assumed positive.

The vocabulary itself is due to Alfred Marshall, who introduced elasticity in his Principles of Economics of 1890 and chose the word for its mechanical analogy: a highly elastic material stretches a great deal under modest force, and a highly elastic supply expands a great deal under a modest price signal. Marshall applied the idea principally to demand, but the same construction transfers directly to supply, and it was Marshall who also insisted that the answer depends entirely on how much time producers are given, a point that turns out to dominate everything else about the measure.

sections.heading: The Formula, and How to Calculate It
sections.body:
The definition is a ratio of proportional changes. Price elasticity of supply equals the percentage change in quantity supplied divided by the percentage change in price. Written for small changes using calculus, it is the derivative of quantity with respect to price, multiplied by price divided by quantity: elasticity equals dQ over dP, times P over Q. That form is called point elasticity and applies at a single point on the supply curve.

For finite changes measured from data, the naive approach creates an awkward problem: computing percentages from the starting point gives a different answer than computing them from the ending point. Suppose price rises from 10 to 12 while quantity rises from 100 to 115. Measured forward, price rose 20 percent and quantity 15 percent, giving an elasticity of 0.75. Measured backward from the new position, price fell 16.7 percent and quantity 13.0 percent, giving 0.78. The standard fix is the midpoint or arc formula, which divides each change by the average of the two values rather than by either endpoint, producing a single number regardless of direction. Here the quantity change of 15 over an average of 107.5 is 13.95 percent, the price change of 2 over an average of 11 is 18.18 percent, and the elasticity is 0.77.

A third approach is often the most useful in applied work. If the supply relationship is assumed to take the constant-elasticity form, quantity equals a constant times price raised to the power epsilon, then taking logarithms gives log quantity as a linear function of log price with epsilon as the coefficient. Regressing the logarithm of quantity on the logarithm of price therefore estimates the elasticity directly, and the estimate applies across the whole range rather than at a point.
steps: State clearly which supply you mean: an individual firm, an industry, a country, or world supply, since these differ by large factors and are routinely confused.
Record two price and quantity pairs that lie on the same supply curve, meaning the movement between them was caused by a shift in demand, not by a change in costs or technology.
Compute the change in quantity and divide it by the average of the two quantities to obtain the proportional change in quantity.
Compute the change in price and divide it by the average of the two prices to obtain the proportional change in price.
Divide the first result by the second; the answer is the arc elasticity over that range, and it is dimensionless.
State the time horizon over which the response was measured, because an elasticity without a horizon is close to meaningless.
Deflate nominal prices by a suitable price index before any of this if the period is long enough for general inflation to matter.
For a curve rather than two points, fit a regression of log quantity on log price and report the coefficient as the elasticity, with its standard error.
Sanity-check the sign: a negative result usually indicates you have traced a demand curve by mistake rather than discovered a perverse supply response.

sections.heading: Reading the Number: Elastic, Inelastic and the Extremes
sections.body:
The dividing line is one. If elasticity exceeds one, supply is called elastic: quantity responds proportionally more than price, so a market absorbs demand shocks mainly through output. If it falls below one, supply is inelastic: quantity responds proportionally less than price, and demand shocks show up mainly in the price. An elasticity of exactly one is unit elastic, and quantity and price move in equal proportion.

Two limiting cases anchor the scale and are worth understanding concretely rather than as abstractions. Perfectly inelastic supply, elasticity zero, means quantity does not respond to price at all; the supply curve is vertical. The stock of land in Manhattan is the standard textbook example, and it is nearly literally true. So is the number of surviving paintings by a dead artist, the number of seats in a stadium on the night of a match, and the quantity of a perishable crop already harvested and sitting in a market that must be sold today. In every such case, a rise in price transfers money to the owner and calls forth no additional supply whatever.

Perfectly elastic supply, elasticity infinite, means producers will supply any quantity at the going price but none at all below it; the supply curve is horizontal. This is the situation of an individual small firm in a perfectly competitive market, which can sell as much as it likes at the market price and nothing at a penny more. It is also the working assumption behind the small open economy in international trade models, where a country can buy any quantity of a world commodity without moving the world price. Neither extreme is ever exactly true, but both are useful approximations that make problems tractable.

Between the extremes, some rough benchmarks help calibrate intuition. Manufactured goods produced in factories with spare shifts available typically show short-run elasticities somewhere between 1 and 3. Agricultural crops within a single season are close to zero once planted and perhaps 0.2 to 0.5 across seasons. Crude oil from conventional fields is famously inelastic in the short run, with many estimates below 0.1, while shale production, which can be drilled and completed within months, has been estimated at several times that. Housing in a constrained metropolitan area may sit below 1 while an unconstrained one exceeds 3. These are orders of magnitude rather than precise constants, and the honest way to use them is as a prior to be revised by evidence rather than as a fact.

One further piece of terminology avoids a common confusion. Elasticity describes movement along a supply curve, caused by a change in the good's own price. A change in input costs, technology, taxes, weather or the number of producers shifts the whole curve to a new position, which is a different event entirely and is not measured by elasticity. Observing that output rose while price fell tells you nothing about elasticity by itself; it tells you that supply shifted outward, and the elasticity governs the shape of the curve that moved, not the movement.

sections.heading: The Geometry of Supply Curves
sections.body:
A result that surprises most people learning the subject is that the steepness of a supply curve does not by itself tell you its elasticity. Consider any straight-line supply curve that passes through the origin, so that quantity equals some constant b multiplied by price. The derivative of quantity with respect to price is b. Elasticity is that derivative multiplied by price over quantity, which is b times P divided by bP, and the b cancels: the elasticity is exactly one, everywhere along the line, regardless of how steep or shallow the line is. Every straight supply curve through the origin is unit elastic.

What determines the elasticity of a straight line is therefore not its slope but where it intercepts the axes. A line that cuts the vertical price axis at a positive price, meaning producers supply nothing until price reaches some minimum, is elastic everywhere, with elasticity greater than one, falling toward one as quantity grows large. A line that cuts the horizontal quantity axis, meaning some quantity would be supplied even at a price of zero, is inelastic everywhere, with elasticity below one, rising toward one as quantity grows. This can be seen directly by writing the line as Q equals a plus bP: elasticity equals bP divided by (a plus bP), which is less than one when a is positive and greater than one when a is negative.

An immediate corollary is that elasticity generally varies along a curve rather than being a fixed property of it. Speaking of the elasticity of supply for a market, without qualification, is loose language; strictly one should speak of the elasticity at a particular price and quantity, or over a particular range. The exception is the constant-elasticity family, quantity proportional to price raised to a fixed power, which is a curve rather than a line and which has the same elasticity at every point by construction. That is precisely why it is so often assumed in empirical work: it makes a single reported number meaningful.

For most real supply curves the elasticity falls as output rises, sometimes dramatically. At low output there is idle equipment, unemployed labour and unused land, and extra production is cheap, so a small price rise brings a large quantity response. As the industry approaches the limit of its capacity, every further unit requires bidding resources away from more valuable uses or bringing worse deposits, poorer land and older machinery into service, and the curve turns steeply upward. Supply that looked highly elastic at half capacity can be nearly vertical at full capacity, which is why capacity utilisation figures are watched so closely as an inflation indicator.

sections.heading: Time: The Dominant Determinant
sections.body:
Nothing affects the elasticity of supply as powerfully as the length of time producers are given to respond, and any elasticity quoted without a horizon should be treated with suspicion. Marshall organised the point into three periods that remain the standard framing.

In the market period, sometimes called the momentary period, output is fixed. Whatever exists has already been produced, and no amount of price movement can create more within the time available. A fisherman's catch on the quayside, a harvested crop at market, a hotel's rooms tonight, the seats on a departing flight: supply is vertical and elasticity is zero, so the entire adjustment falls on price. This is the reason spot prices for perishables and for services with fixed capacity are so volatile.

In the short run, at least one input is fixed, usually the plant, the land or the capital equipment, while others can be varied. A factory can add a shift, run overtime, defer maintenance and buy more raw material, and it can do all of this within weeks. Output can therefore rise, but only by pushing harder on a fixed asset, so the marginal cost of each additional unit climbs and the response is limited. Short-run elasticities are typically positive but modest, and the number depends heavily on how much slack existed at the outset.

In the long run every input can be varied. New factories are built, new wells drilled, new orchards planted, new firms enter and existing ones expand or leave. Long-run elasticity is therefore always at least as high as short-run elasticity and usually much higher, sometimes by a factor of five or ten. How long the long run takes is set by the physical and financial gestation period of the industry, and the range is enormous. Adding a shift at an existing factory takes weeks. Drilling and completing a shale well takes six to twelve months. Planting a coffee tree and waiting for its first commercial crop takes three to five years, and rubber takes about seven. Building a semiconductor fabrication plant takes two to three years and something in the region of ten to twenty billion dollars, which is why the chip shortage of 2021 could not be resolved by price alone. A new deepwater oil field or a nuclear power station takes a decade or more. In each case the gestation lag sets a hard floor on how quickly supply can respond, and no price is high enough to shorten it much.

The practical rule that follows is that any policy or forecast must specify its horizon before quoting an elasticity, and that the same market can look almost perfectly inelastic and highly elastic depending only on whether one is asking about next month or the next decade. Confusing the two is among the most consequential errors in applied economics, because it leads to the belief that a supply response has failed when in truth it has not yet had time to occur.

sections.heading: Capacity, Costs and the Marginal Producer
sections.body:
Beneath the elasticity number sits the shape of the industry's cost structure, and understanding that shape explains why the number takes the value it does. A competitive firm supplies up to the point where the price equals the marginal cost of the last unit produced. It follows that the firm's supply curve is its marginal cost curve above the shutdown point, and that the elasticity of supply is governed by how steeply marginal cost rises with output.
